scenes.title: Cloud Security & Encryption (KMS)
scenes.narration: Cloud key management services like KMS create and control the encryption keys that protect your data at rest and in transit.

scenes.title: Encryption Fundamentals
bullets: Encryption at rest protects stored data so raw disks or objects are unreadable if stolen.
Encryption in transit uses TLS so data cannot be intercepted as it moves between services.
A key management service centralizes key creation, rotation, and access control.
scenes.narration: Two kinds of encryption work together to protect data. Encryption at rest scrambles stored data so a stolen disk or object reveals nothing. Encryption in transit wraps data in TLS as it travels between services. A key management service ties it together by controlling how encryption keys are created, rotated, and accessed.

scenes.title: Envelope Encryption
steps: Encrypted data key is stored alongside
scenes.narration: Cloud services use envelope encryption for scale. A master key stays locked inside KMS and never leaves. KMS issues a short-lived data key that actually encrypts your data, and the encrypted form of that data key is stored next to the data. To decrypt, the service asks KMS to unwrap the data key, keeping the master key safe.

scenes.title: A KMS Key Policy Snippet
scenes.narration: A KMS key policy decides who may use a key and how. This statement allows only the ETL role to decrypt data and generate data keys, following least privilege. By restricting key usage to specific roles, you ensure that even someone with access to encrypted data cannot read it without permission to use the key.

scenes.text: Encrypt data at rest and in transit and control keys tightly through KMS — encryption is only as strong as the access policy on its keys.
scenes.narration: Encrypt everywhere, both at rest and in transit, and treat key access as a first-class security control. Encryption only protects you when the policy governing its keys is equally tight.
